title: Transient peak spike: heap recycling & mitigation notes
content:
Summary:

We see a recurring class of intermittent OOMs on p4d/8xA100 nodes that do not reproduce in synthetic microbenchmarks. Root cause appears to be transient peak-on-path allocation patterns combined with delayed recycling semantics of the CUDA allocator (cudamallocasync and our mempool layers) that leave many small free fragments unusable for the next largest allocation. This doc captures the investigation steps, traces, hypotheses, and recommended mitigations (short- and medium-term).

High-level symptoms observed:
- Sporadic OOMs during multi-session traffic containing long-context requests (>= 16k tokens) mixed with short chat messages. OOM frequency correlates with a subset of requests that trigger KV-cache population followed by concurrent streaming generation.
- GPU memory at process-level shows large amount of free bytes when measured with nvidia-smi ("Free"), but allocations fail at application-level (cudaMallocAsync/cudaMalloc) with out-of-memory.
- Nsight Systems capture shows many small free blocks interleaved with allocated regions; allocator reports (internal counters) show "high free segment count" and "low largest-free-chunk".

Environment snapshot for failing host (example):
- Instance: p4d.24xlarge equivalent, 80 GB GPU RAM per device
- OS/Driver: Ubuntu 22.04, NVIDIA driver 525.x, CUDA 11.8+
- Runtime: serving-runtime v1.9.2, custom arena allocator on top of cudamallocasync

Observations from traces and heap snapshots:
- Timeline (example request):
  00:00 request received -> warm KV-cache allocations (~4.2 GB broken into ~120 chunks, many 32–256 KB sized)
  00:00.2 model init path -> transient peak growth to 68.9 GB (includes attention workspace, key/value caching, activation buffers)
  00:00.6 generation begins -> concurrent streams for token emission touch KV cache and small scratch allocations
  00:01.1 allocation for attention layer expansion (single large allocation ~6.8 GB) fails even though total free memory reported ~10 GB; largest free chunk reported by allocator ~2.1 GB
- Internal allocator logs during failure show fragmentation metric: free_segments=1873, largest_free=2267863552 (≈2.1GB), total_free=11_024_000_000 (≈11GB)
- Free segments are mostly small (<512KB) due to earlier splitting patterns from many small mallocs and the way the slab coalescing is delayed when frees are performed from different CUDA streams.

Key hypotheses (ranked):
1) Delayed coalescing / cross-stream free ordering: cudaFreeAsync and cudamallocasync maintain free lists per-stream or per-chunk, and cross-stream frees are not coalesced immediately, leaving many small isolated free segments that cannot satisfy large contiguous allocations.
2) Workspace sizing policy undershoots required contiguous region for some attention patterns; the runtime grows workspaces in many small increments that fragment the arena.
3) KV-cache allocation granularity is too small; storing KV cache as many small blocks (to optimize reuse) results in internal fragmentation when mixed with large temporary allocations.
4) Host pinned fallback allocations used during spikes are not wired into our coalescing path, causing separate pools to be underutilized.

Experimentation and commands used:
- Heap snapshots: instrumented allocator to emit JSON snapshots at request boundaries. Key script: tools/alloc_dump.py --pid $PID --out /tmp/dumps/request-123.json
- Nsight systems: nsys profile --trace=cuda --sample=cpu --output request-123.nsys ./run_server_trace.sh
- Live allocator logging: set SERVING_ALLOC_LOG=1 to capture path, size, stream id, and timestamp for alloc/free events.
- Repro harness: replay real traffic with recorded requests (reproducer available under tools/repro/kv-seq-heavy.json).

Findings from experiments:
- Replaying the exact request sequence on an otherwise idle GPU reproduces OOM ~90% of runs; when we insert a 50ms gap between KV cache population and heavy workspace growth, the OOM disappears. This points to ordering/timing sensitivity rather than purely capacity.
- Switching to eager coalescing path in our local allocator (aggressively attempt to merge free segments on free regardless of stream context) reduces fragmentation and eliminates the OOM in the reproducible test, but increases latency jitter for frees in microbenchmarks (observed ~1–2ms extra per free in heavy workloads).
- Pre-reserving a contiguous slab (single large cudaMallocAsync reservation at session start) of size equal to expected peak reduces fragmentation but is wasteful for small sessions and increases cold-start memory pressure across tenant pools.

Short-term mitigations (low-risk, incremental):
- Add a small heuristic: when largest_free < required_allocation and total_free >= required_allocation, attempt a targeted background coalescing pass before failing allocation. Non-blocking: mark the allocation attempt as retriable with one coalescing attempt.
- Increase default KV-cache allocation block size for sequences longer than 8k tokens to reduce number of small chunks (change: 32KB -> 256KB chunking for large contexts).
- Add metrics and alerts: free_segment_count, largest_free_chunk_bytes, fragmentation_ratio = 1 - (largest_free / total_free). Alert when fragmentation_ratio > 0.6 and traffic contains long-context requests.

Medium-term mitigations (more invasive):
- Implement a per-GPU "contiguous slab" pool with two modes: reserved-mode for long-context sessions (allocate on first long request, release after session idle for N seconds) and opportunistic-mode where we try to pull contiguous regions from the global pool when needed.
- Improve cross-stream free handling: introduce a delayed aggregation worker that safely coalesces free segments from different streams in a coordinated manner (must respect CUDA stream semantics). This is similar to the eager coalescing but done asynchronously to avoid per-free overhead.
- Provide a server config knob for "aggressive-defrag" which toggles the above behavior per-deployment (hosted customers can opt in/out).

Tradeoffs & risks:
- Aggressive coalescing increases CPU and CUDA stream synchronization overhead; may add latency jitter under certain workloads.
- Pre-reservation reduces memory available to other tenants; must be combined with admission control for Dedicated nodes.
- Any cross-stream synchronization must be carefully validated for correctness with respect to stream ordering and events; incorrect implementation can introduce data races or use-after-free bugs.

Open action items (owners and rough ETA):
- Implement targeted coalescing retry logic (owner: Evan Cho, ETA: 2w)
- Change KV-cache chunking for large contexts and run perf tests (owner: Marina Alvarez, ETA: 1w)
- Add fragmentation metrics + dashboard (owner: Observability team, ticket linked: INF-2384, ETA: 1w)
- Prototype per-GPU contiguous slab pool in feature branch (owner: Priya, ETA: 3w)
- Run 48h soak on staging with mixed real traffic once patches land (owner: SRE, ETA: after PR merge)

Notes and miscellaneous observations:
- This class of problem is sensitive to CUDA driver versions; earlier in the year driver 470.x exhibited slightly different coalescing behavior (fewer free fragments) — worth including driver version as dimension in rollout testing matrices.
- Some customers sensitive to deterministic memory footprints (financial/regulatory) may prefer pre-reservation; offer that as an explicit deployment knob for Private/Dedicated.
- We should add a short section to the Runbook for "oom-with-free-fragments" documenting the minimal diagnostic steps: capture nsys, allocator dump, check largest_free vs required, reproduce with gap insertion test.

Appendix: quick reproducer notes
- Reproducer config: tools/repro/long-kv-burst.yaml (contains request sequence and timings). Run with:
  export SERVING_ALLOC_LOG=1
  ./tools/repro/run_replay.sh tools/repro/long-kv-burst.yaml --device 0
- For deep tracing: nsys profile --output /tmp/trace --trace=cuda,osrt,osrt_mem ./tools/repro/run_replay.sh ...

If this doc looks right I'll open the prototype PR for targeted coalescing and a small perf test harness in the same branch. We should also add a short note in the release candidate checklist to validate fragmentation metrics on all driver builds we intend to ship on.

-- Priya
